performers: Artur Schnabel, piano; London Symphony Orchestra, Malcolm Sargent
intro: Schnabel plays the finale, Allegro vivace assai, of Mozart’s Piano Concerto No. 21 in C major, K. 467, with Sargent conducting. The refrain returns several times between piano runs and short woodwind replies, and a last cadenza comes between the final statement of the tune and the closing bars.

sections.label: A · Refrain in C major, strings then piano
sections.mNote: A short refrain in C major, in two beats.

sections.label: B · Piano runs above held horns
sections.mNote: Connected keyboard phrases lead away from the refrain.

sections.label: A′ · Refrain in C major, piano
sections.mNote: A fermata precedes the return to C major.

sections.label: Dev · Piano and woodwinds exchange refrain figures
sections.mNote: The refrain’s small figures move between instruments.

sections.label: A″ · The C major theme returns
sections.mNote: The piano extends the return with further running notes.

sections.label: Cadenza · Schnabel plays without the orchestra
sections.mNote: A fermata holds the closing cadence open.

sections.label: Coda · Piano and strings, C major
sections.mNote: The refrain returns before the closing C major chords.

cues.title: Refrain and first solo entry
cues.text: The strings introduce a quick C major refrain in two beats to the bar. Mozart breaks off the opening exchange with a pause for the piano, which plays a flourish and then takes up the tune.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, pp. 40–41. Hannah Chan-Hartley describes the refrain, pause and solo flourish: https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36107.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First episode, piano legato
cues.text: The piano plays a connected phrase, marked legato, above held horn notes. Its runs extend beyond the short statements of the refrain. New ideas follow as the first episode modulates away from C major.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, from bar 57, p. 42.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Twelve piano concertos, 1784–1786
cues.text: Between February 1784 and December 1786, Mozart wrote twelve piano concertos. Vienna’s audiences usually heard them with the composer himself at the keyboard. K. 467 was one of the new scores he brought to the platform in 1785.
cues.evidence: Hannah Chan-Hartley, National Arts Centre programme note, gives the date range, twelve concertos and performing context: https://nac-cna.ca/en/event/notes/36107.

cues.title: Return of the refrain in C major
cues.text: After a pause the piano plays the refrain in C major. The orchestra then takes it up.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, bars 169–193, p. 46.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Middle episode, refrain motifs
cues.text: The middle episode breaks the refrain into smaller figures. Piano and woodwinds exchange them in quick alternation, and the piano extends them into longer runs. Each exchange begins with a few notes from the refrain.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, pp. 47–49; Chan-Hartley describes the second episode’s development of refrain motifs.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the refrain, C major
cues.text: The refrain returns in C major and leads into more elaborate piano writing. The strings continue the short phrases beneath the solo part. A cadenza follows later in the movement.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, pp. 50–55: later refrain, solo continuation and cadenza.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cadenza
cues.text: A short orchestral tutti stops at a fermata, and the piano plays alone. The cadenza delays the final cadence and gives Schnabel a longer solo passage after the quick exchanges of the rondo.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, bars 418–423, p. 55. The full score marks the cadenza slot; the recorded cadenza’s authorship is not established in the consulted discography.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Original discs and LP transfer
cues.text: On the original discs the finale fills both sides of a single HMV record, DB 3102, matrices 2EA 4610 and 4611. This stream comes from a later LP transfer, so the movement plays without a break.
cues.evidence: John Bolig, His Master’s Voice Double-Sided Celebrity Recordings, pp. 505–506 (DB 3102, 12 January 1937): https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Bolig2020.pdf#page=530 The LP transfer: https://archive.org/details/Mozart.PianoConcertoNo.21

cues.title: Return of the refrain after the cadenza
cues.text: After the cadenza, piano and strings play the refrain again. Fuller orchestral replies and rising piano scales carry the closing passage towards C major, and trumpets and timpani return for the final chords.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, pp. 55–56, post-cadenza refrain and final cadence.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Held horns beneath the piano
transitions.from: A · Refrain in C major, strings then piano
transitions.to: B · Piano runs above held horns
transitions.how: The orchestral refrain closes in C major. The piano resumes with a legato phrase over sustained horn notes, and the strings rest at first. Over this lighter scoring the soloist extends the tune into a more continuous run of notes.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, bars 51–73, p. 42.

transitions.title: A fermata before the refrain
transitions.from: B · Piano runs above held horns
transitions.to: A′ · Refrain in C major, piano
transitions.how: Piano runs over held string notes lead to a fermata on the dominant of C. After the pause, the piano plays the refrain in C major over the strings, and the orchestra then repeats the tune.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, bars 169–193, p. 46.

transitions.title: Orchestral continuation leaves C major
transitions.from: A′ · Refrain in C major, piano
transitions.to: Dev · Piano and woodwinds exchange refrain figures
transitions.how: The orchestral continuation takes the refrain away from C major. Short piano phrases alternate with woodwind phrases, each taking up fragments of the tune and repeating them at different pitches. The two-beat Allegro continues through these changing keys.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, pp. 47–49; Hannah Chan-Hartley, National Arts Centre programme note.

transitions.title: Dominant link to the piano’s return
transitions.from: Dev · Piano and woodwinds exchange refrain figures
transitions.to: A″ · The C major theme returns
transitions.how: A short orchestral link holds G, the dominant of C major. The piano then takes up the refrain again over the strings. The two-beat phrase returns unchanged, following the broken exchanges of the middle section.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, bars 307–315, p. 50.

transitions.title: Fermata on the cadential six-four
transitions.from: A″ · The C major theme returns
transitions.to: Cadenza · Schnabel plays without the orchestra
transitions.how: The orchestra plays a short tutti and stops on a C major chord over a bass G (bars 418–423). The fermata holds this cadential six-four unresolved. Schnabel played the cadenza alone, and then piano and strings resume the refrain.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, bars 418–423, p. 55.

transitions.title: Piano and strings restore the refrain
transitions.from: Cadenza · Schnabel plays without the orchestra
transitions.to: Coda · Piano and strings, C major
transitions.how: The cadenza leads back to the refrain in C major, with the piano above the strings’ regular accompaniment. Winds, brass and timpani join the closing passage. Rising keyboard scales carry the music to the final cadence.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1878), Broude reprint, III, pp. 55–56.

source.title: Mozart, K. 467, full score: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1878; Broude reprint, plate 422
source.locator: III. Allegro vivace assai, printed pp. 40–56: refrain, episodes and the cadenza marked on p. 55.

timeline.note: Strings introduce the refrain before the fuller orchestral answer.
Upper winds answer the violins, with brass and timpani reinforcing the cadences.
After the pause, the piano plays the refrain over light strings.
The piano begins a legato phrase over held horns; the strings enter again in reply.
The piano plays the refrain again above the strings, then passes it back to the orchestra.
Winds and strings carry the orchestral link into the middle episode.
Piano runs alternate with short woodwind replies and brief string accompaniments.
The piano extends the returning refrain. Trumpets and timpani reinforce the intervening orchestral phrases.
The orchestra rests while Schnabel prolongs the unfinished cadence.
Piano and strings resume the refrain after the cadenza.
Full orchestral replies and rising piano scales lead to the final C major chords.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Artur Schnabel (piano), London Symphony Orchestra (orchestra), Malcolm Sargent (conductor)
fields.note: The item, source LP sleeve and LSO discography identify the same performers. Bolig identifies the piano as a Bechstein. The honorific Sir belongs to the later source wording and is not used to date Sargent’s knighthood.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition is not identified. The Schnabel chronology credits his cadenzas for K. 467; the consulted orchestral score shows the finale’s cadenza slot but not the performed cadenza text. No internal cadenza themes or exact bar alignment are asserted. The Archive states that the former file mix-up with K. 595 has been corrected; attribution here follows the corrected item, without claiming independent aural authentication.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The LSO register dates K. 467 to 12 January 1937, separately from K. 459 on 9 and 12 January. Both finale matrix entries carry 12 January in the side-level discographies.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: The Archive names Abbey Road Studios; the LSO, Bolig and Schnabel records specify Studio 1.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Angel Records — Great Recordings of the Century
fields.note: Angel is the label of the mono LP explicitly identified as the transfer source. The original 1937 issue was on His Master’s Voice.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The catalogue number appears on the photographed cover. The LSO discography dates this LP reissue to November 1959 and the complete original HMV set DB3099–3102 to November 1937. The finale occupied the two sides of DB3102.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Probable original-side lineage: 2EA 4610-2A and 2EA 4611-2A; finale parts 1–2 on HMV DB3102, concerto sides 7–8.
fields.note: These are documented issued takes in Bolig and the Schnabel chronology; their presence in the particular Angel LP transfer is inferred rather than established by runout inspection or take comparison. The LP pressing and its own matrix/runout are unknown. No original side-join timestamp is claimed. A targeted DAHR search did not produce a usable session record, so no DAHR matrix entry is cited.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item explicitly states ‘Transfer by Bob Varney’, separately from its uploader metadata.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item’s 19 April 2010 added date and the current file’s later timestamp do not identify when the LP was digitised. The correction notice is not a dated transfer log.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No playback equipment, equalisation, denoising, editing or speed-correction procedure is supplied. The VBR MP3 original-upload descriptor identifies the digital submission, not a session master or an unprocessed transfer.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mozart’s concerto, and Schnabel’s authorship of the credited cadenzas, are beyond the ordinary life-plus-70 term.
fields.note: Mozart died in 1791 and Schnabel in 1951. Under the ordinary life-plus-70 calculation, Schnabel’s authorship term ended in 2021. The consulted orchestral score derives from the public-domain 1878 edition. This is not worldwide clearance of unidentified editorial material or a conclusion about US cadenza publication history.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: territorial — EU public-domain basis: first published in November 1937 on HMV DB3099–3102.
fields.note: The LSO discography expressly documents the 1937 publication, rather than merely the recording session. Its ordinary EU 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected at that date. The package relies on this territorial basis only. US status is not established, and the recording does not meet the publication-by-1925 cutoff. The uploader’s http://creativecommons.org/licenses/publicdomain/ declaration is recorded as source metadata, not independent proof of authority to release the performers’ or producer’s rights worldwide. The legal URL below is the term basis, not a Creative Commons grant.

composer.epithet: Composer of operas in which a servant outwits a count, and of piano concertos in which the soloist sometimes enters before the orchestra has finished its opening.
facts: He usually called himself Wolfgang Amadè Mozart
Childhood tours across Europe; three Italian visits, 1769–73
His home from 1781; concertos, quartets and the Da Ponte operas
K. or KV: Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and revised since

quote.text: In an opera, poetry must simply be music’s obedient daughter.
quote.source: Mozart to his father Leopold, Vienna, 13 October 1781; our translation

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to play the finale through. The work was K. 466 in D minor. It opens with syncopated strings, and the piano enters with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert excellent.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart later dedicated the quartets to him.
